analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun makers and dealers by repealing the industry's legal immunity.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 4, 2025 with 114 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law since 2005 — the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act — blocks most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, sellers, and their trade associations over harm caused by the criminal misuse of a firearm. This bill repeals that shield, so victims and their families could sue in state or federal court like they can against other products. It also lets lawyers in those cases obtain and present ATF firearms trace data, which currently cannot be forced out in civil suits.
analysis.who_benefits: People shot or injured by guns, and families of those killed, gain the right to sue manufacturers, sellers, and dealers whose distribution practices — such as supplying traffickers or negligent dealers — put guns in the hands of shooters. They also gain access to ATF trace data to prove those patterns in court.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which bars civil actions against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm [S2] [S3].

Makes the ATF's Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and discovery, admissible as evidence, and usable in civil actions and administrative proceedings in any state or federal court, on the same basis as other information [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations would lose their near-total protection from civil suits and could face litigation, discovery, settlements, and judgments; those costs could be passed on to gun buyers through higher prices and liability insurance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade groups

drawbacks.text: The repeal covers suits for damages resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm, so sellers of legally functioning products could face lawsuits over crimes committed by third parties, not only over defective products [S2] [S3].

Opening the Firearms Trace System database to discovery puts detailed law-enforcement tracing data into civil litigation, which defendants and some law-enforcement officials have historically argued could expose sensitive investigative information [S3].

Defensive litigation costs and liability insurance in the gun trade would likely rise, and those costs tend to be passed through to prices paid by ordinary gun owners — the standard effect of expanding civil liability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims, the gain is real: today the 2005 law leaves them without the ordinary right to hold a negligent seller or manufacturer accountable in court, a protection available for virtually every other consumer product. The main costs fall on the gun industry and, through higher prices and insurance, on lawful gun buyers. The strongest objection is that liability reaches conduct a seller did not directly commit — a crime by a third party — but the bill does not create liability automatically; plaintiffs would still have to prove a legally culpable connection in court.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits in the House Judiciary Committee, which has held no hearing, markup, or floor vote on it since its June 2025 referral.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Swalwell introduced the bill on June 4, 2025, with 57 original cosponsors named in the bill text [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and the complete action history shows no further action since [S5].
114 of 217 House Democrats had cosponsored the bill as of the latest cosponsor list [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations keep the litigation immunity they have held since 2005, and victims and their families remain unable to sue over harms from criminal misuse of firearms. Supporters' effort is not yet dead — Congress is still in session — but the bill has not moved since referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry keeps its lawsuit shield

for.name: Rep. Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 4, 2025 and shepherded it to committee referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its June 4, 2025 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history.

against.name: National Rifle Association and firearm trade associations
against.what_they_did: Have long championed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act and opposed congressional efforts to repeal it.

sides.party_line_note: All 114 cosponsors are House Democrats and no Republicans sponsor or cosponsor the bill, so support runs entirely on one side of the aisle [S4].

industries.industry: Gun and ammunition manufacturers and dealers
industries.note: The bill repeals the federal shield that since 2005 has barred most civil suits against them for harm from criminal misuse of firearms. The legal accountability victims would gain is precisely the litigation exposure the industry would lose [S2] [S3].

The Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act also protects trade associations from these suits; repeal ends that protection and opens them to being sued over industry marketing and distribution practices [S2].
Repealing the liability shield would create demand for new liability coverage across the gun trade, adding premiums — costs that tend to be passed to gun buyers.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a Republican-held House, and no committee action three months after referral, the bill is likely to remain in the Judiciary Committee without a markup or floor vote this Congress, as PLCAA-repeal bills in prior Congresses have.
